verdict.reasoning: Independently confirmed on every checkable particular, though the claim understates the scope by two orders of magnitude. (1) PDF page 326 (printed folio 296) was rendered at 300 dpi: the heading '12.3.7.4   General rules' is present near the bottom of the page, set bold, following general rule 32) and preceding general rule 1) 'All clauses specified in the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph...'. Quoted correctly. (2) The markdown lines were read directly and every line number and heading level in the claim is exact: 13875 '## 12.3.7 SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph', 13878 '### 12.3.7.1 General', 13903 '## 12.3.7.2 General format', 14025 '## 12.3.7.3 Syntax rules', 14217 '## 12.3.7.4 General rules'. So 12.3.7.4, a four-component clause number, carries the same h2 rank as its own three-component parent 12.3.7, while its sibling 12.3.7.1 correctly carries h3. (3) This is NOT a lost-text finding and NOT reflow/hyphenation/page-break furniture: the heading text is fully present and verbatim correct, and no prose is missing. The defect is purely the markdown heading rank, i.e. the encoded document hierarchy. I count it real because the clause numbering itself is decisive - 12.3.7.4 is by definition a subdivision of 12.3.7 - and because the file's own dominant convention agrees: of the four-component headings in specs/ISO_COBOL.md, 620 are correctly '###' against only 162 at '##' (and 24 at '####'). An h2 for a four-component number under an h2 parent is objectively inconsistent with both the numbering and the transcription's own norm, and it flattens the subtree in any generated outline or TOC. (4) One part of the claim's rationale does NOT survive scrutiny and should not be relied on: it is not the case that the PDF visually distinguishes these ranks. Page 319 was rendered and '12.3.7 SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph' and '12.3.7.1 General' print at near-identical bold size and indent; page 320's '12.3.7.2   General format' is typeset identically to page 326's '12.3.7.4   General rules'. ISO's own typography does not separate depth 3 from depth 4 here, so the rank must be inferred from the clause number, not from the printed glyphs. The claim's phrase 'printed at the same rank as 12.3.7.1/.2/.3' is therefore true but proves less than it implies - those siblings are printed at the same rank as the PARENT too. (5) The proposed repair scope is wrong. The defect is not confined to the three headings of 12.3.7: the immediately adjacent siblings '## 12.3.6.4 General rules' (line 13790) and '## 12.3.8.4 General rules' (line 14599) carry it as well, and file-wide 162 four-component headings sit at h2. This is a systemic OCR/structuring defect, so a three-heading sweep would leave 159 instances behind.
verdict.corrected_description: REAL, but mis-scoped and partly mis-argued. Confirmed: specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 14217 renders '12.3.7.4 General rules' as '## ' (h2), the same rank as its own parent '## 12.3.7 SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph' at line 13875, flattening the 12.3.7 subtree in any generated outline. No text is missing or altered - the heading string is verbatim correct against the rendered PDF page 326 - so this is a heading-rank/hierarchy defect, not a lost-content defect. Two corrections to the claim: (a) the PDF does not typographically distinguish depth-3 from depth-4 clause headings (rendering pages 319, 320 and 326 shows 12.3.7, 12.3.7.1, 12.3.7.2 and 12.3.7.4 all set in the same bold face and size), so the correct rank is established by the clause NUMBERING and by the transcription's own dominant convention (620 four-component headings at '###' vs 162 at '##'), not by any visible difference in the printed glyphs; (b) the sweep is far larger than the three headings named - '## 12.3.6.4 General rules' (line 13790) and '## 12.3.8.4 General rules' (line 14599) share the defect, and 162 four-component headings sit at h2 file-wide. The repair should be a single mechanical pass promoting every N.N.N.N heading to h3 (and re-checking the 24 at '####'), not a hand edit of 12.3.7.2/.3/.4.
